newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Veil of secrecy hides health of Vietnam president.
newsitem.headline: Veil of secrecy hides health of Vietnam president.

text.p: Vietnam's President Le Duc Anh was reported to be unconscious in a Hanoi hospital on Sunday after being admitted with blood pressure problems, but there were conflicting indications about the severity of his condition.
Staff at Hanoi's 108 Army hospital confirmed the 75-year-old president was being treated in a special wing assigned to top cadres, but would not provide details of his condition.
A hospital medic said President Anh had fallen ill over the past week but his health had since improved. He added that Anh might be discharged soon.

But government officials who declined to be identified, gave a more bleak picture of the situation and indicated it was far "It's really serious," one said. "They've started to make the preparations (for his death)."
Separate government sources said Anh was unconscious. One said an unusually wide gap between his upper and lower blood pressure readings was making his condition difficult to treat.
The president was also said to be suffering haemorrhaging around the brain.

But an apparent veil of secrecy was being drawn across the situation on Sunday obscuring further information about Anh's health. Presidential aides and advisers could not be contacted by phone. Several were said to have cancelled engagements. Official media made no mention of his condition.

State television, apparently reading from a foreign ministry news schedule issued several days ago, said on Sunday that Anh and his wife would be meeting with South Korea's President Kim Young-sam, who are due to visit later this week.
Hanoi's political rumour mill had been awash with speculation about the president's health over the past week because of a longer than usual absence from public view.
An informed political source said on Sunday Anh had undergone a routine health check-up earlier in the week but was then readmitted to hospital on Friday.
Newspapers reported he had signed a decision formalising changes to Vietnam's cabinet as recently as November 12.
General Anh is one of three top leaders in Vietnam and was appointed president in September 1992.
He is seen by Western observers as representing the conservative and military elements of Vietnam's communist government and is ranked number two in the elite politburo.
The next most senior politburo member from a military background is 64-year-old Lieutenant-General Le Kha Phieu.
Anh, a battle-hardened soldier and veteran of Vietnam's campaign in Cambodia during the late 1970s and 1980s, occupies a key position in the communist country's leadership.
Presidential influence over the estimated 572,000-strong military is seen as a part of the mechanism by which close party-army ties are ensured.
The other members of the ruling triumvirate are Communist Party chief Do Muoi, 79, who is viewed as occupying a central and stabilising role in government, and Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet, 73.
Kiet is widely viewed as a strong backer of the market-oriented economic and social reforms introduced 10 years ago in place of the former Soviet-style command-led system.
